overview: Spicy's Parkour auto-jumps at block edges. On every pre EventUpdate it requires the player to have existed for at least one tick, the MovementUtils ground probe with a 0.000000001 tolerance to report the player touching support, the block below the current position to be air, and the block below the previous tick position to be solid; when all four hold it calls mc.thePlayer.jump(). The last-tick solid and current air pair is the edge detector, so the jump fires on the same tick a manual parkour jump would. The module adds no velocity: the jump is the vanilla method and its wire effect is the ordinary C03 jump motion of the next tick.

sections.p: The module is one pre EventUpdate branch with five conditions. ticksExisted must be greater than 0, MovementUtils.isOnGround(0.000000001) must report the player grounded, the block at the current foot position minus one must be air, and the block at the previous tick's foot position minus one must be solid. When all five hold, mc.thePlayer.jump() fires. There is no onDisable handler and no state beyond the settings-free module, so the branch is stateless from tick to tick apart from the world and the player's own fields.

The last-tick solid plus current air pair is the edge detector: the player was standing on support one tick ago and is already over the gap now, which is exactly the tick a manual parkour jump would happen. The tiny 0.000000001 tolerance deserves the note: isOnGround(0.000000001) offsets the bounding box down by one nanometer, so it is true only while the player is essentially touching support, and it keeps the module from jumping mid-air or during the landing arc. The jump is the vanilla method, so the resulting motion is a normal jump with no added velocity.

The module sends no packet directly; the jump manifests on the wire as the C03 jump motion of the next tick. Its countering surface is therefore the movement checks that validate jump envelopes and horizontal deltas, and none of those sees a difference between this jump and a manual one, because the physics are identical. The module only removes the human timing requirement.

files.label: Parkour.java (module)
files.explanation:
The module is one pre EventUpdate branch with five conditions: the player has existed for at least one tick, MovementUtils.isOnGround(0.000000001) reports the player grounded within a billionth of a block, the block at the current foot position minus one is air, and the block at the previous tick's foot position minus one is solid. When all hold, mc.thePlayer.jump() fires. The last-tick solid plus current air pair is the edge detector: the player was standing on support one tick ago and is already over the gap now, which is exactly the tick a manual parkour jump would happen.

The tiny 0.000000001 tolerance deserves the note: isOnGround(0.000000001) offsets the bounding box down by one nanometer, so it is true only while the player is essentially touching support, and it keeps the module from jumping mid-air or during the landing arc. The jump is the vanilla method, so the resulting motion is a normal jump with no added velocity.

The module sends no packet directly; the jump manifests on the wire as the C03 jump motion of the next tick. Its countering surface is therefore the movement checks that validate jump envelopes and horizontal deltas, not anything that reads module state.

files.label: MovementUtils.java (ground probe)
files.explanation:
MovementUtils is the shared utility class Parkour calls for its ground probe. isOnGround(double height) offsets the player's bounding box down by height and returns true when getCollidingBoundingBoxes reports any collision; the two-argument overload does the same for an arbitrary player, and canStep wraps the same probe with a horizontal-collision check for step logic. setMotion converts a speed and yaw into motionX and motionZ with the standard forward-strafe composition.

Parkour uses only the single-argument probe with the 0.000000001 offset, so the file's other helpers, setMotion, canStep and the player overload, are dead weight for this module but are embedded because the generator reads the whole file. The probe is world-state driven: it reads the collision boxes of the client world, not the packet onGround flag, which is why the edge condition is accurate to the actual geometry.

The file is shared across Spicy's movement modules, so the same probe semantics appear in the module's siblings; only the calling pattern differs.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (jump envelope)
countering.explanation:
SurvivalFly rebuilds the client's vertical motion from the world rather than trusting the packets. In check() the vertical allowance comes from vDistRel, which initializes from the previous move's momentum and accepts only named envelopes: a zero-y move on ground, a jump, a step-up and a riptide launch, with ground state taken from the block cache instead of the packet's onGround flag. Anything outside those envelopes produces a yDistanceAboveLimit and a set-back.

Parkour's jump is a vanilla jump by construction: the module calls mc.thePlayer.jump() on the tick the player stands on the last solid block with the block below the new position already air, so the resulting C03 carries exactly the upward motion vanilla would produce from a grounded jump. SurvivalFly's jump envelope accepts that motion, which is why a single parkour jump never flags; the module is timing-only and adds no vertical gain.

The boundary: the check bites the failure mode, not the jump itself. If the parkour jump is chained into a speed or bhop pattern, the following moves leave the accepted envelopes, through extra horizontal or vertical gain or air-jumps without ground contact, and the set-back fires. A plain Parkour user who jumps edge to edge stays inside the envelope the entire time.

countering.label: Speed (horizontal envelope, Hawk)
countering.explanation:
Hawk's position Speed check measures the horizontal delta of each MoveEvent against the allowed envelope for the player's movement mode, punishing breaches through the standard rubberband path. It is the horizontal counterpart to SurvivalFly in this countering set.

Parkour does not add horizontal speed: it triggers the jump at the edge tick, and the client's own physics convert the forward input into the arc. The horizontal component of that arc is ordinary running motion, so the per-tick deltas sit inside the envelope and the check passes while the module is on. It stays relevant because parkour modules are often bundled with speed enhancement, and the extra horizontal gain then pushes the same edge-jump moves past the envelope.

The boundary: the module's jumps are indistinguishable from legitimate parkour play in horizontal terms, and this check has no vertical component, so it neither confirms nor denies the jump itself. Detection of the module requires a check that cares about jump timing or vertical consistency, which this one does not.

countering.label: Speed (horizontal envelope, Arc-v2)
countering.explanation:
Arc-v2's Speed check applies the same horizontal-envelope model, with ice, ice-block, block-move and step modifiers against configurable maxima, to the reported deltas, punishing what the player's movement mode cannot justify. Like Hawk's Speed, it is content-blind to why the player is moving.

The relationship to Parkour is identical in shape: the jump arc is vanilla physics, the horizontal deltas stay at running speed, and the check passes while only the module is active. The entry documents the enforcement that applies the moment the session adds horizontal speed cheating on top of the automatic jumps.

The boundary: no horizontal speed check can detect Parkour by itself, because the module never changes the player's speed envelope. The honest summary is that the countering set for this module protects against the escalation, not the feature; the feature is a legitimate-motion jump that vanilla and every envelope-based anticheat accept.
